lesson.title: When More Data Does Not Help: The Meaning of Bias
lesson.summary: Bias is a systematic tendency for a sampling or study method to produce results that are consistently too high or too low, a flaw that collecting a bigger sample cannot fix because it is built into the method itself.
lesson.body:
In statistics, bias refers to a systematic tendency of a sampling method, a survey, or a study design to produce results that miss the true value of a population characteristic in a consistent direction, rather than scattering randomly above and below it. This is a very different problem from ordinary sampling variability, which is the natural, random fluctuation that occurs simply because a sample is not the whole population. Sampling variability shrinks as the sample gets larger, because a bigger sample tends to average out to something closer to the truth. Bias does not shrink with a larger sample size at all, because the flaw is baked into how the data are collected, not into how much data are collected.

This distinction connects directly to two ideas already introduced. Bias is the reason careful attention must be paid to how a sample is drawn, since a sample is only useful as a stand-in for the population if the method that produced it does not systematically favor certain outcomes. It is also the reason observational studies require such careful scrutiny, since many common study designs, from surveys to volunteer based data collection, contain sources of bias baked into how participants end up being observed at all.

A worked example makes the shrinking-sample-size point vivid. Imagine a phone survey conducted only using landline telephone numbers, asking people about their political opinions, and imagine the survey collects responses from 500 people. Because landline ownership skews toward older, often more established households, and younger adults disproportionately rely on cell phones only, this method systematically under-represents younger voters in every single sample it could possibly draw. If the survey were repeated with 5,000 people instead of 500, using the exact same landline-only method, the results would settle down to a very stable number, but that stable number would still be wrong in the same direction, since the underlying method still shuts out the same group of people every time. More data made the estimate more precise, but not more accurate, which is the hallmark of a biased method.

It is worth being careful with the vocabulary here, since students often use accuracy and precision interchangeably even though statisticians do not. Precision describes how much a statistic would vary from sample to sample if the same method were repeated many times; bias describes whether that statistic is centered on the true population value or centered somewhere else entirely. A method can be highly precise and highly biased at once, consistently landing near the same wrong answer every time, which is arguably more dangerous than a method that is imprecise but unbiased, because a biased method can look deceptively trustworthy due to its consistency.

Recognizing bias is therefore not about complaining that a sample was small or that results varied a little; it is about asking whether the method that generated the data had a structural reason to favor one kind of answer over another. That question, who or what got systematically left out or overrepresented, and why, is the starting point for evaluating almost any real world survey or study, and it sets up the specific, named sources of bias covered next.
